messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marcus Cole had served twelve years in the infantry before the Army Medical Board retired him at thirty-four. He still remembered the exact sequence in Kandahar: the dry heat of the patrol, the sudden crack of small arms, and the way the earth threw up a wall of dust and diesel fumes. A young squadmate had been pinned behind a concrete culvert. Marcus had crouched low, his rifle heavy in his hands, his breath coming in short, sharp pulls. He remembered the distant thrum of a rotorblade cutting through the air—a search pattern crossing the valley. He had stayed pressed into the dirt, waiting for a clear window that never came. His friend had survived, but the window had closed, and the weight of that hesitation stayed with him. The memory did not fade; it arrived with a clarity that startled him. He would be refueling his truck at the state park service depot and suddenly catch the phantom scent of burnt rubber and wet cordite. The recollection would flood his mind, so vivid and immediate that the present moment seemed to flatten, leaving him detached, as though he were observing himself from a distance. He was uncomfortable in those moments, a cold tension tightening his chest until the sensation passed. He had come to believe that permanent damage had been done to him, that the man who could step outside without his shoulders hunched was gone forever. When he returned to the states at forty-three and took a position as a park ranger, the landscape felt deceptively open. The ranger station sat at the end of a winding gravel road, its reinforced windows offering a clear line of sight to the visitor entrance. Marcus positioned his chair near the east-facing desk, his body angled to take in both the trailhead and the tree line. He was certain that if he stopped scanning the perimeter, something would slip through. He watched the parking lot, tracking the posture of every visitor who approached the information kiosk, noting how they carried their bags, how quickly they moved. Unexpected noises—a truck backfiring on the service road, a hawk diving through the pines—sent his pulse into his throat. He had come to believe he had to be on guard all the time. The memories of the ambush felt more real to him than memories of ordinary things; they carried a weight that ordinary recollections never did. When maintenance crews flew over the ridge in light aircraft, he would step into his SUV, roll up the windows, and sit in silence until the sound faded. He started taking his lunch breaks in the employee break room with the blinds drawn. The habit of staying behind glass and closed doors formed over months. His presence at home shifted accordingly. His wife, Elena, noticed he stopped joining her on evening walks along the creek. He would sit on the porch instead, his posture rigid, his gaze fixed on the darkening tree line. He told himself he was resting, but he knew it was the guilt that kept him tethered to the ground, the unshakable conviction that he would never forgive himself for what he had left undone. The tension, the guilt, and the watchfulness simply occupied the same days. By forty-six, the weight had settled into his bones. He sought counseling after a routine trail inspection turned into a prolonged episode of stillness when a search-and-rescue helicopter passed overhead. He had gripped the steering wheel until his knuckles whitened, his breathing shallow, his attention locked on the sky. He came to the clinic hoping to find a way back to the man he was before, or at least to quiet the constant alarm ringing in his head. What he hoped for most was simply to walk the trails without his hand hovering near his belt, to sit at the dinner table without his ears tuned to the sky, and to believe, even for a moment, that the past had finally stopped watching him from the present.
